title: RACI x Systems Thinking
author: PM Researcher
summary: PM Researcher Nicole synthesizes two recent academic pieces—an HBR article on RACI decision-rights frameworks and a Comenius University qualitative study on systemic project management—to surface the same underlying mechanism in both: organizational change does not happen when a leader declares a new state from the top, but when a local behavioral pattern is reproduced with enough fidelity, in enough places, that it becomes the system's new default. The HBR finding is that RACI fails in practice when treated as a static artifact filled out by a senior leader and handed down; buy-in must be co-created with the people who will actually live with the assignment, clarifying what accountable and responsible mean in behavioral terms at the level of each specific decision. The Comenius study, grounded in Luhmann's systems theory, adds that even holistic frameworks like systemic project management must be piloted locally before they can scale—organizations do not adopt complex theoretical frameworks on faith, they reproduce them repeatedly in ordinary conversation until the pattern becomes ambient. Nicole's synthesis is that most change efforts fail by picking one end of this mechanism and ignoring the other: pure local iteration never generalizes without deliberate spread, while holistic rollouts without a bounded starting point produce the very inertia they were meant to overcome. The practical sequencing she extracts: pick a real bounded decision, build the new behavior with the people who will use it, get it right locally, then treat generalization as an ongoing communicative act rather than a one-time announcement.
points: The RACI framework fails in practice not because the tool is bad but because it is typically deployed as a static artifact—a senior leader fills out a spreadsheet and expects compliance—when it only works when co-created with the specific people who will live with it, specifying what accountable and responsible mean in behavioral terms for each particular decision.

Systemic project management research, drawing on Luhmann's systems theory, shows that acceptance is not a decision made once but a pattern that gets anchored in organizational communication and continuously reproduced in everyday work—which means adoption is fundamentally a communicative act, not an approval event.

Both pieces converge on the same underlying mechanism: global organizational order is an emergent property of local rules repeatedly applied, not something imposed from the top; what looks like holistic change from a distance is just local iteration viewed from far enough back.

Change efforts fail at two failure points—pure local iteration that never generalizes because no one built the muscle to spread the pattern, and holistic rollouts without a bounded starting point that collapse under the weight of their own abstraction before a single team changes behavior.

The practical sequencing both pieces support: pick a real bounded decision, build the new behavior with the people who will use it, get it right locally, then treat generalization as an ongoing communicative act—because the moment people stop actively reproducing the new pattern in conversation and practice, it reverts to the organizational default.
quotes: You can’t mandate a system into changing. You can only change how it behaves one decision, one team, one conversation at a time and hope the pattern holds long enough to become the new normal.
People don’t play assigned roles just because a document says so. Buy-in has to be built, and it has to be built at the level where the actual decision lives, not declared from three layers up.

Clarify the specific goal before assigning roles. Co-create the RACI with the people who’ll live with it. Write out what “accountable” and “responsible” actually mean in behavioral terms, because half the time people in the same room are using the words differently.

acceptance isn’t a decision anyone makes once. It happens when a new way of thinking gets “anchored in organizational communication and continuously reproduced in everyday work.” Not approved. Reproduced. Repeatedly, locally, until it’s just how people talk to each other.

Neither of these findings is really about RACI or about automotive project management. They’re about the same underlying mechanism showing up in a governance tool and in a cultural framework: systems don’t change because someone at the top declares a new state. Change happens because a local pattern gets repeated with enough fidelity, in enough places, that it becomes the system’s new default behavior.

Global order is an emergent property of local rules, not something imposed from outside the system. What’s useful about lining up an HBR governance article with a systemic-PM academic paper is that you get the same mechanism validated in two completely different registers: hard-nosed management consulting on one side, systems-theory academic research on the other. When practitioners and theorists converge on the same answer from different directions, that’s usually a sign the answer is actually right, not just fashionable.
Holistic change was never the alternative to local iteration. It’s what local iteration looks like once you’re standing far enough back to see the whole system doing it consistently.
